analysis.one_liner: Bans the largest online platforms from using manipulative designs to trick users into sharing personal data.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and stayed there until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The DETOUR Act would make it illegal for online companies with more than 100 million users to design their sites and apps in ways that trick people into handing over personal information or agreeing to things they didn't mean to agree to — the so-called 'dark patterns' like confusing yes/no buttons or pre-checked boxes. It would also require companies to get informed consent before running behavioral or psychological experiments on groups of users, and to ban design features that push children under 13 into compulsive use, such as video autoplay. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rules, and companies would have to disclose their experiments to users every 90 days and set up independent review boards for research on their users.
analysis.who_benefits: Hundreds of millions of people who use large social networks, search engines, and email services. The bill's main protections target deceptive interface design that pushes users into sharing data or consenting to things, behavioral experiments run on users without real consent, and addictive-by-design features aimed at children under 13.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Users of the biggest online platforms

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits large online operators from designing or manipulating a user interface with the purpose or substantial effect of obscuring, subverting, or impairing user autonomy, decision-making, or choice in order to obtain consent or user data [S3].
Prohibits segmenting users into groups for behavioral or psychological experiments without the informed consent of each user involved [S3].
Prohibits designing interfaces directed at children under 13 that cultivate compulsive usage, explicitly including video auto-play initiated without user consent [S3].

Requires companies to disclose every 90 days which experiments or studies users were subjected to or enrolled in for engagement or product conversion, and to establish an independent review board, registered with the FTC, with power to approve, modify, or disapprove behavioral research on users [S3].
Enforces violations as unfair or deceptive practices under the FTC Act, with FTC rulemaking within one year of enactment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The largest online companies — social networks, search engines, and email providers with over 100 million monthly users. They would have to redesign interfaces to remove manipulative patterns, end or get consent for user experiments, and run registered review boards and disclosures. Some compliance cost could ultimately show up in products, and ordinary A/B testing of layouts and text would be restricted unless covered by the bill's de minimis safe harbors.

drawbacks.text: The bill lets an association of large online operators register with the FTC as a professional standards body and gives companies a safe harbor from FTC enforcement if they relied in good faith on that body's guidance — industry-run self-regulation could blunt the law's force [S3].

The independent review boards would be formally designated by the large online operator itself, so genuine independence from company management would depend on FTC rulemaking that was never written [S3].

The prohibition on interfaces that impair 'user autonomy, decision-making, or choice' turns on a company's purpose or substantial effect, a standard that could sweep in ordinary interface testing beyond clearly deceptive practices; the bill's safe harbors for de minimis changes only partially address this [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are real and aimed at practices — deceptive consent flows, hidden experiments on users, addictive design for young children — that companies have shown little willingness to fix on their own. The main weaknesses are structural: much of the enforcement architecture runs through industry-created standards bodies and company-designated review boards, with an enforcement safe harbor attached. A stronger version would have relied more directly on FTC rulemaking. Still, the core bans on deceptive design and non-consensual user experiments are direct and enforceable.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the same day, and the committee never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Mark Warner (D-VA) introduced S. 1084 on April 9, 2019, joined by Senator Deb Fischer (R-NE) as an original cosponsor [S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day of introduction [S5].
No further action was ever taken: the bill received no committee consideration, no floor vote, and was never taken up before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].
The bill ended with three cosponsors — two Republicans and one Democrat — and died in committee [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest online platforms are better off because the bill died: their freedom to use interface designs that maximize data collection and engagement, and to run behavioral experiments on users without informed consent, was never restricted. Users, especially children, got none of the bill's protections.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from day one — a Democratic sponsor paired with a Republican original cosponsor, ending at two Republicans and one Democrat — but no vote was ever taken, so the bill never faced a recorded partisan test.

industries.industry: Large online platforms (social networks, search engines, email providers with 100M+ users)
industries.note: The bill bans the interface designs these companies use to push users into consenting and sharing data, requires consent for user experiments, and bans compulsive-use design for children under 13. Because the bill died without a vote, none of these restrictions took effect.

industries.industry: Advertising-driven attention economy (engagement research and A/B testing operations of big tech)
industries.note: The bill would have required 90-day disclosure of engagement and product-conversion experiments and independent review board approval, while preserving de minimis layout testing and offering a safe harbor for industry-standards-body guidance. Engagement research that depends on manipulating user choice would have been the most constrained; the industry's interest in keeping that research undisclosed runs against users' interest in knowing when they are being experimented on.
